idiom_name: sealed interface state hierarchy + exhaustive when decider + coroutine withTimeout
implementation_notes: The classic state-object structure collapses into a sealed interface hierarchy plus a pure when decider, so every transition is checked for exhaustiveness at compile time - adding a state without handling it is a compile error, not a runtime surprise. suspend functions with withTimeout (or select on channels) express deadlines, and one coroutine actor per instance serialises events without locks. What the language does not provide is durability: the state is a value persisted in a row (Exposed, JPA) and the outgoing command is written to an outbox in the same transaction, which remains hand-written. The classic, table-driven form is still justified when the flow is large enough to want a declarative definition or a framework-provided persistence layer.
pitfalls: Sealed states are for the decision only; storing the collected business data inside them recreates a god object, so keep a separate context value alongside the state.
A coroutine per instance is only safe if exactly one actor consumes that instance's events; collecting the same channel from several coroutines breaks the state invariant.
withTimeout cancels the awaiting coroutine but not the remote operation it started, so a timed-out step can still complete and must be idempotent.
Persisting with a suspend call inside the when-branch mixes decision and I/O, making the decider untestable; keep the branch pure and perform persistence around it.
